Foto: Yle / Mapcreator Här är fastighetsköpen som Finland stoppat – Sverige saknar liknande lag Uppdaterad idag 05:47 Publicerad idag 05:44 Fastigheter nära kritisk infrastruktur, osannolika affärsplaner och köpare med kopplingar till rysk elit. Finland har stoppat 68 fastighetsaffärer sedan 2022 med hänvisning till säkerhetsrisker. I Sverige hade köpen sannolikt genomförts. SVT Nyheter har tidigare berättat att svenska myndigheter saknar en generell möjlighet att stoppa utländska fastighetsköp , med hänvisning till nationell säkerhet. Trots varningar från Säpo och nästan tio års utredning. Frågan har blivit aktuell i Sverige sedan Försvarsmakten velat ta över en fritidsfastighet nära en marinbas i Stockholms skärgård. I Finland ser det annorlunda ut. Landet har skärpt sina regler för fastighetsköp av utländska medborgare, utanför EU. ”Vi kommer inte tillåta affärer om det inte går att utesluta ett hot mot den nationella säkerheten”, säger försvarsminister Antti Häkkänen till Yle . Totalförbud för ryssar Fram till den 1 september i år har 68 fastighetsaffärer stoppats i Finland. Sedan juli 2025 råder dessutom i princip förbud för ryska och belarusiska medborgare att köpa fastigheter. Enligt Rickard Lindholm, sakkunnig på finska försvarsministeriet, handlar det om att förebygga säkerhetshot. Ryska staten kan tvinga medborgare utomlands att agera i Rysslands intresse. – Vi vill förhindra att det på lång sikt uppstår ett massivt fastighetsägarskap som skulle kunna användas i en eventuell konflikt. Stoppar inte rätt personer De finska lagarna fyller en viktig funktion enligt Kari Liuhto, professor i underrättelseforskning vid Finlands försvarshögskola. Misstänkta köp kan stoppas i ett tidigt skede. Att använda expropriering är både svårare och mer kostsamt, säger han. Men samtidigt anser han att lagarna fokuserar för mycket på medborgarskap. – I de flesta fall stoppar vi inte rätt personer, konstaterar Kari Liuhto. Enligt honom använder rysk underrättelsetjänst mellanhänder, eller andra metoder, om den vill komma över en strategiskt viktig fastighet. – De flesta ryska fastighetsköp i Finland har inget med underrättelseverksamhet att göra. Risken ökar Finska myndigheter är medvetna om risken för köp via bulvaner, och att den risken ökat sedan ett år tillbaka, när ryska köp stoppas helt. – Vi har möjligheter att ingripa mot misstänkta bulvaner, men utmaningen är att hitta dem, konstaterar Rickard Lindholm på finska försvarsministeriet. Trots luckor i lagstiftningen anser han att säkerhetshotande fastighetsköp ändå försvåras, eftersom köp granskas. – Den avskräckande effekten är det mest centrala. Livsmedlen försvinner snabbt LRF har i en fingerad modell räknat ut hur snabbt vanliga livsmedel tar slut, om importen stryps. Tomatodlingen i Ljustorp i Timrå kommun ligger på samma breddgrad som Finlands tomtacentrum Närpes där mer än hälften av Finlands omkring 34 tusen ton tomater produceras. Skillnaden är markant om man jämför med Sverige där produktionen är hälften så stor och i Norrland minimal. Enligt Jordbruksverkets statistik fanns bara 25 tomatodlingar i hela Norrland 2023. Baksidan är svårigheten i att få lönsamhet, Eva Hörnström efterlyser stöd och rådgivning av experter för att hitta balansen i produktionen. – Det är svårt att själv räkna på hur man ska kunna effektivisera, säger hon. Sverige vill minska EU-stöd Forskaren Henrik Haller anser att det är rimligt med stöd till jordbruket, samtidigt oroar sig LRF över att Sverige driver på i EU för ett minskat jordbruksstöd. – Det skulle försvaga den svenska livsmedelsproduktionen, säger Mikaela Johnsson. sources.summary: Kvinnan som dödades i fredags arbetade med att hjälpa ungdomar. Hon dog efter att ha blivit skjuten på en idrottsanläggning och händelsen har lett till stor oro. – Det är klart att det känns väldigt, väldigt obehagligt, säger justitieminister Gunnar Strömmer (M).

Hon dog efter att ha blivit skjuten på en idrottsanläggning och händelsen har lett till stor oro. – Det är klart att det känns väldigt, väldigt obehagligt, säger justitieminister Gunnar Strömmer (M). Många i området kände den 25-åriga kvinnan som sköts till döds i Älvsjö i södra Stockholm i fredags. Hon arbetade med unga inom kommunens ungdomsverksamhet och sköts på övervåningen av en idrottsanläggning. Samtidigt var hundratals ungdomar på plats i en närliggande idrottshall där det pågick både fotbollsmatch och innebandymatch. – Det är klart att man känner ett stort obehag, säger justitieminister Gunnar Strömmer (M). Han säger att det är särskilt allvarligt när den här typen av våldsdåd sker mitt i samhället där andra människor rör sig, speciellt där barn vistas och berörs. Ännu är motivet bakom skjutningen oklart och de två minderåriga som gripits misstänkta för mordet nekar till brott. Möjligt hämndmotiv Enligt uppgift till SVT ser polisen hämnd som ett möjligt motiv, då en nära anhörig till kvinnan funnits med på en så kallad ”dödslista” . – Exakt vad det här är, och hur vi ska förstå det, är lite för tidigt för mig att säga, men jag har stor förståelse för att många känner sig berörda, säger Strömmer och fortsätter: – Jag har förstått att det här var en väldigt uppskattad medarbetare i stadsdelen, att det är en person som många idrottsföreningar har en relation till. Det är klart att det här framförallt är en stor tragedi för den unga kvinna som skjutits ihjäl och hennes familj. Samhället måste kliva fram Det är inte ovanligt att våldsdåd mot anhöriga leder till hämndaktioner. Men enligt Gunnar Strömmer är för tidigt att säga om det här brottet riskerar att leda till en våldseskalering i närtid. – Vi får avvakta och se vad man kommer fram till. Arbetet för att få boende i området att känna sig trygga menar Strömmer nu handlar om närvaro och om samspelet mellan polisen och kommun, genom stadsdelsförvaltningen och civilsamhället. – Samhället tillsammans måste i ett sånt här läge kliva fram, säger Gunnar Strömmer. sources.title: A wave of homemade, synthetic drugs sweeps US and deepens crisis
sources.summary: BBC News hears from users, dealers, prison and recovery workers as the country battles with a deadly new drug epidemic.
sources.text: Figure caption, The BBCâs Quentin Sommerville joins officers at Cook County as they carry out an early morning raid By Quentin Sommerville International correspondent, Columbus, Ohio Published 18 October 2026 Warning: This story contains descriptions of drug-taking from the start and discusses suicide The few grains of fentanyl sit in the silver foil as a straw, held between Mike's lips, hovers above, with a cigarette lighter below. The 48-year-old army veteran is crouched low in an alleyway in Columbus, Ohio's Linden neighbourhood. "This drug will damn near make you do anything, unfortunately," he says. The hit he's smoking cost three or four dollars. "You can snort too much and you can't take it back. Kind of like a gunshot. Can't call the bullet back," he says. He burns the foil and inhales. As the opioid takes hold, he grips the fence behind him. He sways as a low moan comes from deep in his throat - he could be humming a tune. We've spent a few days with Mike - he's been our guide through the neighbourhood's back streets. Everyone seems to know him and he's regarded fondly. He helps out at a local pawn shop and gas station, and that's how he feeds his 20-year-old opioid addiction. Synthetic opioids are more powerful and in plentiful supply, and they have transformed the drugs landscape. Fentanyl, which is entirely man-made, is 50 to 100 times more powerful than heroin, which is cultivated from poppies. It is now often cut with synthetic tranquillisers, which make reviving overdose victims more difficult. These are homemade threats, where cocktails of synthetics can be made in American basements and bathtubs. America's War on Drugs: The Synthetic Wave Extraordinary access shows how strong synthetic drugs are changing America's drug crisis. Watch on iPlayer Image source, Darren Conway/BBC Image caption, "This drug will damn near make you do anything, unfortunately," says Mike as he lights up a few grains of fentanyl Image source, Darren Conway/BBC Image caption, Mike, a former army veteran, acts as our guide through the neighbourhood's back streets We have Naloxone (brand name Narcan) in our pockets, in case anyone on our team comes into contact with fentanyl or anyone around us overdoses. It's a nasal spray that immediately reverses opioid overdoses and its widespread adoption has transformed the number of fatal overdoses in the United States. At its peak in 2022, 110,000 Americans were dying from overdoses, mostly from opioids. The number has been dropping since, down to around 70,000 last year. But that doesn't mean the opioid crisis is over. It's likely that the reversal drug in my pocket, which has saved tens of thousands of drug users' lives, would not have worked on Mike. Because he wasn't just smoking fentanyl. The pupils in his milky blue eyes shrink to pin pricks. "Opioids make your pupils go smaller, but not that small," he says in a singsong voice. Even the fentanyl, dangerous enough on its own, has other synthetics added. When we ask what he thinks his drugs have been cut with, he replies: "Xylazine, and the one we can't pronounce." Medetomidine is what he means. Like xyalzine, it is also referred to as tranq and both are synthetic animal tranquilisers. "Large animal tranquilisers," as one recovery expert told me. They help prolong the high from the fentanyl but are a sedative that slows breathing and, importantly, naloxone doesn't work against them. Xylazine also causes necrotic skin ulcers, wounds so deep they can make it down to the bone and are difficult to treat. Recovery group offering hope At the Glenwood Church on the other side of town, members of the Hope Dealer Community, a recovery group, gather for a weekly meeting. For many, their struggles are written in their care-worn faces, and their eyes are those of survivors of a great trauma. They take to the stage at the front of the church and share their stories with a brutal and courageous honesty. One man tells the story of his overdose in July 2022. Two paramedics worked on him, trying to save his life. He had naloxone drips in both arms. They hit him with the opioid reversal three times to no avail. "That's it, I'm gonna call it," said one of the medics. But the other insisted on one more try, and it was that which saved his life. As the crowd shouts encouragement, Tonya takes to the lectern. She recounts how her nephew died of an overdose while she was overdosing at the same time from crack cocaine, a stimulant spiked with fentanyl, a synthetic opioid. "It's not luck. I'm supposed to be here," she says with tears in her eyes. The audience yells its agreement. Image source, Darren Conway/BBC Image caption, Members of the Hope Dealer Community, a recovery group, gather for a weekly meeting at Glenwood Church Image source, Darren Conway/BBC Image caption, One of those gathered at the church, Tonya, recounts how her nephew died of an overdose while she was overdosing at the same time Both in Columbus, and later in Chicago, we would hear of crack cocaine users who had died of overdoses after their drugs contained fentanyl. On the street, it's called a "hot dose". "In the last 12 months in Franklin County [Columbus], 78% of fatal overdoses are from stimulants," explains Scott Sanders, 65, who runs Hope Dealers. Scott is almost 10 years sober, a powerfully built man in his early 60s with an electric energy. When he asks the room to raise their hands if anyone has overdosed, most of the gathering does so. "The crisis has just shifted," Scott tells me afterwards. "The tragedy is stimulant users who are purchasing crack think that's what they're getting, and they're not. They're getting crack mixed with fentanyl or other opioid cocktails and overdosing without being aware of it." Image source, Darren Conway/BBC Image caption, Scott Sanders, 65, is almost 10 years sober and runs Hope Dealers Overdose deaths among black men in Ohio are actually increasing, he adds. His organisation works with the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) on a drug sampling programme. Participants bring their needles or pipes for swabbing and the samples are sent to the CDC's laboratory in North Carolina. That's how we learned that Mike's instincts were right, he likely wasn't just smoking fentanyl. One of the drug kits he brought in tested positive for medetomidine. "The drug supply in 2026 is this: we think we are buying crack but we're not, we're buying a number of different things," says Scott. "Today it is mixed, not just cut, but mixed with other drugs such as fentanyl or meth, and then other adulterants chemicals that are made in basements." And it was basement-made synthetic drugs that would cause a dramatic increase in overdose deaths one state over, in Illinois. Watch the documentary on YouTube , external I meet a dealer in Chicago who works for the Mexican cartels selling fentanyl. He would only speak to us if we agreed to mask his identity. Challenged on his role in the 50,000 people dying each year because of the opioid crisis, he says he knows it is wrong. But when asked why he keeps doing it, he said the end justifies the means. He told me that despite the latest efforts by the US government to target the cartels by declaring them terrorist groups and labelling fentanyl a weapon of mass destruction, his supply chain is as strong as ever. When I ask him if the targeting of boats containing suspected traffickers by the Trump administration has made any difference, he replies that his product is still getting through from Mexico. "If it doesn't go over the wall, it goes under the wall. If it doesn't go through the border, it comes through the top border. This game is about adaptability." And when I asked what has changed in his business, his answer was clear. "Synthetics. We haven't seen... what synthetics can do yet. It's not even the tip of the iceberg," he tells me. A novel approach Chicago's largest jail, one of the largest jails in America, is Cook County. Traditional drugs were usually brought into the jail in body cavities, so the jail had the same body scanners you find at airports to prevent that happening. "In 2023, all of a sudden we saw a spike in overdose deaths, but then hand in hand with that we saw, around persons that had either passed away or people we revived, paper all over the place," explains Sheriff Tom Dart, who runs the jail. "We were seeing paper that was being burned and all of this was completely novel." The facility, which averages one or two overdose deaths a year, lost eight inmates that year to fatal seizures. Security footage shows prisoners spasming and collapsing. It also showed them lighting paper in microwaves in the cell block kitchens. It was indeed, as Dart said, a novel approach. Drugs were being mailed into the jail soaked in the pages of books and in letters. "Cannabinoids and being soaked in a range of other things that were then subsequently lit on fire and inhaled to get high", the sheriff explained. Cannabinoids, sometimes know as K2, are an entirely synthetic version of a cannabis plant extract. They are extremely dangerous and were to blame for the fatal seizures. Image source, Darren Conway/BBC Image caption, In Chicago's largest jail, drugs were soaked in the pages of books and in letters In August, I joined Dart's corrections officers as they prepared for an early morning raid on the jail's high security D block. Around two dozen officers tread lightly and speak in hushed tones as they gather outside the block door. "Don't let them hear you. Silence, silence," commands one of the officers leading the search. As the officers rush in, I smell burning paper in the air and can hear the sound of toilets flushing, presumably as contraband is hurriedly disposed of. As the search gets under way, the focus is on any paper in the cells - the books and letters belonging to inmates. The detainees are escorted to a holding area as the cells are turned over. Every scrap of paper in the rooms is checked by the officers. There are burn marks on the vents in many of the cells, where inmates place smoulder tapers that allow them to ignite the drug-soaked paper. Now every piece of post that enters the jail is scanned for moisture. Somewhere between a quarter and a fifth of all packages and letters test positive and are rejected. Image source, Darren Conway/BBC Image caption, Between a quarter and a fifth of all packages and letters that enter the jail test positive for moisture Outside the jail's walls, it's not hard to encounter the effects of the synthetic drugs wave on Chicago's streets. In the west of the city, day and night, men and women are bent double, swaying, as Mike did, as fentanyl and other synthetics surge through them. In the upscale Oak Park neighbourhood, the local metro station has a vending machine that dispenses naloxone for free. Nearby, a gaunt-looking man in a wheelchair has deep wounds in his legs, likely from xylazine use. He's being tended to by 40-year-old Karen Bell. Karen is a recovery worker with the group Liv4Lali. A former heroin user, she's 17 years free from hard drugs. She exudes kindness, and when I ask her about the drugs being used now, she says, "so many things are being mixed in right now. And it's affecting our bodies, whether it's the wounds, whether it's the withdrawals - and sometimes wounds can extend to the point where it's life changing." Her organisation, like Hope Dealers in Columbus, distributes test strips which check drugs for fentanyl, medetomidine, xylazine and other adulterants. The drugs now, says Karen, are "way more dangerous". "Because before, back in my day, I stopped using heroin 17 years ago, right. That was still heroin. When you bought that you knew it was heroin. But now, when you buy a bag, you don't know really what it is," she tells me. Image source, Darren Conway/BBC Image caption, Karen, a recovery worker, tends to a gaunt-looking man in a wheelchair in an upscale part of town Dart has been sheriff of Cook County for 20 years, so I ask him how the war on drugs was progressing. "I don't think there's anybody involved with it who would sit there and say it's a raging success. It's not," he tells me. And the new problem, he says, reiterating the Chicago drug dealer, is synthetics. "The tradition has always been that law enforcement had an even more vital role because everything that was potent was coming across the border, whether it was coming from Colombia, Mexico, China, the poppy fields of Afghanistan. Now, with the explosion of synthetic drugs, people can do this in their house, in their sink, in their bathtub, you name it." Victory in the war on drugs won't come from focusing just on the supply side, the sheriff adds. "Front and centre there's got to be huge substance abuse treatment," he says, mentioning a number of recovery programmes running in his jail. "You can reduce the market if you can address people's issues with substance abuse. And I know many people who, after long struggles, have come out on the other side in a really good way." 'A lot of people are struggling' Karen knows how difficult it is to quit. She was still using heroin when she got pregnant with her daughter, Abby, now 17. After our meeting at the metro station, I meet them both in a country park in a suburb outside Chicago. With typical care, Karen tells me to watch out for the poison ivy as we walk along a muddy track. It wasn't far from here, around 17 years ago, that she was at her lowest ebb. Image source, Darren Conway/BBC Image caption, Karen says her pregnancy was an opportunity to get clean. She's 17 years free from hard drugs As the wind blows through a tall oak tree beside us, she says: "The day I found out I was pregnant, I was on my way to commit suicide. I was so fed up with trying to quit. I was so fed up with living in a tent in the woods, using a bucket. I was so fed up with losing my friends and family because I was just so ashamed." A pregnancy test changed her mind

sources.title: France's government under pressure after weekend of widespread violence
sources.summary: Political tension grips France after rioting marred protests over the cost of living and struggling public services, Katya Adler writes.
sources.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, President Emmanuel Macron urged calm in his national address following widespread looting and violence By Katya Adler Europe editor ,Â Reporting from Paris Published 46 minutes ago France's Prime Minister SÃ©bastien Lecornu is holding a crisis cabinet meeting on Monday to assess a weekend of violence and looting across the country, in what were some of the worst scenes of public disorder in modern French history. On Saturday over half a million mainly peaceful protesters demonstrated against rising living costs and dwindling access to decent public services, including a good state education. But the protests turned nasty after groups of black-clad, masked activists and vandals appeared. An estimated 1,500 shops and businesses were looted and destroyed. Riot police fired tear gas and turned water cannon on crowds. They were seen hitting people with batons in several places. France's interior ministry said about 1,000 police officers were injured on Saturday, seven of them seriously. There had been rumours in France that President Emmanuel Macron may introduce a temporary curfew in parts of the country, or even impose a state of emergency to help calm the febrile atmosphere. In the end, he used a televised address to the nation on Sunday to call for national unity and to try to assure the French public that the perpetrators of the violence would be punished. Macron's speech has been roundly criticised on social media forums and by political opponents for lacking concrete detail. How will vandals and rioters now be brought to account? How might France's towns and cities be better protected - especially since new mass demonstrations have been announced in a couple of weeks' time? Exactly how will destroyed businesses be compensated? And when will a dialogue be established with students and teachers' bodies on the subject of education? Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, Vandals defaced Statue de la Republique in central Paris over the weekend On Sunday the Secretary General of the CGT union, Sophie Binet, accused Macron of failing to address students' concerns, the cost-of-living crisis or the dwindling quality of public services in France. He's apparently passed that baton to Prime Minister Lecornu. Yet he and his interior minister are charged by many in France with being woefully ill-prepared and under-policed ahead of Saturday's multiple, scheduled protests. The president of France's lower house of parliament, YaÃ«l Braun-Pivet, says she wants to open an inquiry into exactly what happened this weekend and why. "Things are dark in the city of light [a nickname for Paris]" was the graffiti I read daubed in red paint across a wall adjacent to a row of shattered shops in the French capital on Sunday night. Macron is widely viewed here as a lame-duck president. He is on his way out. There's a hotly contested race under way to become his successor, with the vote scheduled in six months' time. The presidential candidate from the anti-immigration nationalist right (Marine Le Pen) and also the anti-capitalist left (Jean-Luc Melenchon) are vying to make headlines. That is adding to current tensions in France - in politics as well as on the streets. Parliament here is paralysed, deeply divided between three vying political blocks. Then there are France's financial woes too. Investors are leaning hard on this country to get its spiralling public debt under control. But the French government worries, if it cuts public services or welfare, yet more angry people will pour out onto the streets. What now, what next, is our country broken? You hear these questions a lot at the moment. People across France were shocked and troubled by Saturday's events. The images of tear-gassed towns, apparently unimpeded looters and burning public buildings have worried the nation. Figure caption, 'Very upsetting': Residents in shock after historic French town hall set alight Many passers-by I speak to express frustration that, while they worry about the future, their leading politicians seem, instead, to be passionately focused on finger-pointing; blaming one another for the volatility. "While we worry for our safety, they use this situation as a pre-presidential election political football," teacher and father of three Edouard told me. Macron and his prime minister blamed Saturday's violent chaos on radical far left groups and delinquents; hard left leader Jean-Luc Melenchon alleged government "incompetence"; Marine Le Pen on the nationalist right, which likes to be seen as strong on law and order, posted a video seated in front of the French flag, giving a presidential-style address blaming the "Macronist administration that is out of steam, exhausted, and disoriented". For the next two weeks, the French authorities hope for a bit of a respite. Students start their half-term break as of Monday. But on 5 November, a cross-section of trade unions, plus France's disparate "yellow jacket" (gilets jaunes) movement that staged demonstrations for over a year in 2018 - during Macron's first term as president - have announced huge protests. France is holding its breath. sources.title: Major fire at Canada military base leaves four dead, dozens injured
sources.summary: Prime Minister Carney said military and emergency crews fought the flames throughout the night in "some of the worst conditions imaginable".
sources.text: Figure caption, Carney: 'Canada must now serve' service members killed in fire By Jessica Murphy ,Â Canada digital editor Â and Â Nadine Yousif ,Â Senior Canada reporter ,Â Reporting from Edmonton Published 5 hours ago Four members of the Canadian military have died and dozens were injured in a major fire at a base in the province of Alberta. Addressing the nation on Sunday from Ottawa, Prime Minister Mark Carney described it as "one of the worst tragedies for the forces on Canadian soil in peacetime". The fire broke out at about 16:00 local time (22:00 GMT) on Saturday at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, one of the country's busiest military training bases, and is now contained. Its cause is still unclear, but officials said it did not appear tied to "terrorist activity". "The nation is in mourning for those brave members of our armed forces who we have lost," said Carney. The BBC has confirmed that Sgt Morgan Wong, Pte Shaun Farrell, Pte Aidan Goulding and Pte Hayden Lykkemark have died. Of the 39 injured people being cared for in hospital, at least 19 are in a critical condition, Alberta Premier Danielle Smith said at a press briefing on Sunday evening. Fire and rescue teams are remaining at the scene to contain any potential flare-ups, Wainwright Mayor Bruce Pugh told the BBC. Members of the infantry had been conducting "high-intensity combat training with live munitions" at a grenade range and attack range, where 10 soldiers practise attacking a simulated enemy, Maj-Gen Wade Rutland told reporters at the briefing. "There was a multitude of ordnance moving through the Wainwright training area," he said, including a grenade launcher, grenades, small arms and ammunition. A grass fire ignited about 1km (0.6 miles) away, with the cause currently under investigation, and moved toward the attack range. "What I would say is there was multiple training activities happening throughout the training area at the time," he said. "Uncommonly strong winds caused the fire to spread rapidly and shift direction towards the range administrative area." Figure caption, Watch: Incident at Canadian military base 'unheard of', says local mayor Cannon fire had been heard coming from the base on Saturday before it suddenly stopped, Mayor Pugh told the BBC, noting it's not uncommon to hear cannons being fired there. News then came through that local emergency services had been deployed to an "all hands on deck" situation. Carney said military and emergency crews fought the flames throughout the night in "some of the worst conditions imaginable". The people who were hurt were on the attack range and included reservists and soldiers from the Princess Patricia's Canadian Light Infantry, officials said. In a statement early on Sunday, the Canadian Armed Forces said that "while the incident remains under investigation, at this time, there are no indications that it was the result of any terrorist activity". Rutland told the briefing: "We do not believe this [incident] to be a result of any oil and gas infrastructure nor any outside interference". What we know so far about deadly fire at Canadian military base Published 4 hours ago Wainwright, about 210km (130 miles) east of Edmonton, Alberta's capital, is one of the main bases used by the Canadian military for live-fire training exercises, and it houses troops from Canada and allied countries. About 690 military personnel and 300 civilian workers are on site on a typical day. Warren Thirsk, an emergency department doctor at the Royal Alexandra Hospital, told broadcaster CBC that the number of patients involved in the incident had "completely overwhelmed" healthcare facilities in Wainwright. The Royal Alexandra Hospital is in Edmonton, where patients are being transferred. The hospital at first declared a code orange - a disaster-response protocol for a high-casualty incident. That has since been stood down. Image source, EPA Image caption, Wainwright is about 200km (125 miles) from Edmonton, the provincial capital The provincial health agency said in a statement on Sunday that it deployed 30 units directly into Wainwright, including 22 ground ambulances, six fixed-wing and two rotary wing units. "It is anticipated that care for patients impacted by this incident will be intensive and will add to existing high demand on acute care in Alberta," it said, adding that patients were being treated at facilities across the province. STARS, the regional air ambulance service, said aircraft and crews from Edmonton, Saskatoon, and Calgary had been deployed. Brandon Simmons, who lives in long-term care at the Wainwright Health Centre, told Reuters that when code orange was announced, nurses dropped everything and immediately started grabbing stretchers, gurneys and medical equipment before running to the front entrance. Ambulances kept coming "throughout the night", he said. sources.summary: French President Emmanuel Macron gives a national address after widespread disorder and as some looting continued in Paris.
sources.text: Figure caption, Watch: James Waterhouse speaks to looted shop owners on the streets of Paris By Jack Burgess Published 18 October 2026 French President Emmanuel Macron has called for "calm and order" after a major day of protests turned into rioting and looting on Saturday, and as some disorder continued in Paris on Sunday. In a national address from the ÃlysÃ©e Palace, he warned those who had taken part not to "escalate", adding: "We all feel anger and shame." Some 550,000 demonstrators took to the streets for largely peaceful protests against rising fuel prices, the cost of living and deteriorating public services, including schools. Macron said a distinction must be drawn between the "legitimate demands" of protesters and "those who destroyed, smashed and looted". Police have arrested about 2,400 people, according to France's interior ministry. The French president said "nothing justifies" the "unbridled" violence seen and said those involved would face justice. Groups of rioters, some dressed in black and wearing masks and balaclavas, also came out in Paris, Marseille and other towns and cities, with some setting fire to cars and buildings. Figure caption, 'Very upsetting': Residents in shock after historic French town hall set alight On Sunday, looting and clashes with police continued on a smaller scale in parts of the capital and Lyon. Tear gas and stun grenades were fired at hundreds of people in Paris, according to the AFP news agency, and bottles and rocks were again hurled at police. Sunday saw cities across the country confront the impact of what developed into one of the worst bouts of disorder in modern French history. In Limoges, the ornate 19th Century city hall was gutted by a fire started by rioters on Saturday, its clock tower and roof collapsing and the flames took hold. Image source, Mairie de Limoge Image caption, A view of the damage inside Limoges town hall on Sunday morning Speaking near the ruined building, AnnÃ¨yse said: "This is very upsetting. Harming heritage buildings just because you are angry at the government is selfish, I think. It's hurting everybody." "It's awful and unbelievable," said another man who gave his name as Gerrard. "We are very sad and I think it will be a long time to put it back as it was before." Shopkeepers were seen early on Sunday morning picking up large shards of glass in Paris as rubbish trucks cleared up debris on some of the larger streets. Image source, Reuters Image caption, Fires were lit and shops looted during smaller scale disorder in Paris on Sunday Widespread looting took place across the cities of Paris, Marseille and Lille, as well as other areas. Macron said local prefects and mayors would draft measures to protect shops and civic buildings. The president also said there would be "full transparency" over the police response to the demonstrations. Tear gas and water cannon were turned on crowds over the weekend and riot police were seen hitting people with batons in several places. France's interior ministry said about 1,000 police officers were injured on Saturday, seven of them seriously. Image source, Reuters Image caption, A man tries to extinguish a fire in Paris on Sunday Student protests which began last month escalated significant on Saturday after they were joined by trade union members and other anti-government groups. The response from political figures has pointed to France's deep political divisions as the country prepares for an election in April which could see the hard-right pitted against the hard-left. France's Interior Minister Laurent NuÃ±ez said that while demonstrating was a fundamental right, there were "outrages" committed by "several thousand far-left individuals" who were determined to target public buildings and confront the police. Later, they were joined by "delinquents who looted and ransacked numerous businesses in several cities in France", he said. Jean-Luc MÃ©lenchon - leader of the hard-left La France Insoumise party - heavily criticised NuÃ±ez and police chiefs on social media. He said they had "shown complete incompetence" with their handling of the demonstrations and called them "specialists in organised chaos". Meanwhile, the leader of the hard-right National Rally party, Marine Le Pen, condemned the "exploitation" of anger "by political forces that encourage violence". Anton Källberg förlorade en tajt EM-final – efter att ha blivit utklassad i det avgörande skiljesetet. – Det kändes bra, förutom i de två sista seten då jag är i princip chanslös, säger en besviken silvermedaljör till SVT. Tidigare under söndagen skrällvann Anton Källberg mot tyske världselvan Dang Qiu i semifinalen. Frågan var om den svenske 29-åringen skulle orka ladda om till finalen bara några timmar senare mot storfavoriten och världstvåan, fransmannen Felix Lebrun, 20. Svaret var ja. Källberg spelade fokuserat och tog hem det första setet med 11–7. Redan i andra set tvingande Källberg den unge fransmannen att förbruka sin timeout efter att ha tagit fyra raka bollar vid ställningen 10–5 till Lebrun. ”Timen” gav dock effekt och Lebrun skrek ut sin glädje efter setvinst med 11–9. ”Hur stark är han mentalt?!” Källberg, rankad 29:a i världen, spelade varierat och överraskade Lebrun flera gånger med långa servar. Trots att svensken spelade bra pingis vann Felix Lebrun det efterföljande setet med 13–11. Men Källberg reste sig återigen och kvitterade till 2–2 i set. – Hur stark är han mentalt?! frågar sig J-O Waldner retoriskt i SVT:s sändning. Finalen utvecklade sig till en förstaklassens nagelbitare. Källberg tog hem det femte setet med 11–9 och var bara ett set från ett historiskt EM-guld. Nära första svenska guldet på 26 år 2000 vann Peter Karlsson EM-guld i Bremen. Sedan dess har inte en svensk herrspelare vunnit EM i singel – och nu hade Källberg chansen att ta det första svenska EM-guldet på 26 år. Men, med kniven mot strupen gjorde Felix Lebrun sina två överlägset bästa set i matchen och vann de två avslutande seten med 11–6 och 11–1. ”Ska vara jättestolt” Anton Källberg åker från Slovenien med två EM-silver. I går förlorade han dubbelfinalen i par med Kristian Karlsson mot Felix och Alexis Lebrun. – På förhand hade man tagit två silvermedaljer, men just nu är det tråkigt. Det hade varit så fint med ett guld, säger Källberg. – Fantastiskt. Första singelfinalen och han står upp här och det har varit tuffa matcher hela vägen. Han har jobbat stenhårt från början av turneringen till nu. Han ska vara jättestolt över det han gör här, sammanfattar den svenska förbundskaptenen Michael Maze Anton Källbergs EM. Damernas final vanns av ryskan Elizabet Abraamian efter att hon besegrat tyskan Annett Kaufmann med 4–3 i set. Jag kände att jag måste gå ut och visa att jag bryr mig, säger hon. Sabah Göranzon beskriver Kämpetorpshallarna som en plats där det brukar vara fullt med barn och ungdomar, liv och rörelse. Suzan Habib som bor i området beskriver den första känslan som oro och chock. – Jag börjar tänka på min egen tonåring som nyss gått på den skolan. Så det känns ju väldigt nära, säger hon när hon besöker platsen. – Det här önskar man ju inte någon ungdom. Det är supertråkigt att de ska behöva vara med om det här, säger Suzan Habib. ”Hammarby Fotboll i sorg” Många unga var på plats i lokalerna på fredagskvällen eftersom det pågick en innebandymatch och en fotbollsmatch arrangerad av Hammarbys Samhällsmatchen, som beskrivs som Hammarbys samhällsprojekt. ”Flera anställda inom Hammarby Fotboll har arbetat tillsammans med henne och känner henne väl, och det är med stor bestörtning vi tagit emot beskedet”, skriver föreningen på Instagram . Det är en fruktansvärd händelse och alla våra tankar går till familjen, anhöriga och medarbetarna i vår organisation, säger Lee Orberson, stadsdelsdirektör i Hägersten-Älvsjö. Enligt SVT:s utsända reporter har nya spänningar uppstått mellan demonstranter och polis i Paris under söndagen. I första arrondissementet i centrala Paris var det på söndag morgon omöjligt att hitta en enda orörd butik, rapporterar Le Parisien . Tobakshandlare, skönhetssalonger, apotek – alla hade krossade rutor, graffiti eller andra tecken på förstörelse. I hela landet uppges mellan 550 000 och 800 000 personer ha deltagit i lördagens protester , som började som en studentrörelse men vuxit till att involvera många olika grupper. Demonstrationerna har i stort varit fredliga men under lördagen urartade de i vad Le Figaro beskriver som ”urban gerillakrigsföring”. Även från städer som Marseille, Lyon, Bordeaux, Montpellier och Nice rapporteras stor förstörelse. – Jag trodde aldrig att jag skulle se något liknande. De har förstört vårt arv, säger en invånare i Limoges, där stadshuset från 1800-talet brann, till Le Figaro. På söndag eftermiddag har nya spänningar uppstått mellan demonstranter och polis i Paris. Enligt SVT:s utsända reporter Tomas Thorén skringras maskerade demonstranter med tårgas på Place de la République.
